details:
SPHEREx Blink (COSMIC EYE) – Project details

Nov 15, 2026 · @Deena Dhayalan .G

SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool where anyone enters a sky position and watches every SPHEREx image of that patch play in time order, like a short video, to look for moving objects. Challenge: Planet X and SPHEREx, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Summary (short description)

SPHEREx images the whole sky in 102 infrared colours (0.75–5 µm), so a single patch of sky is seen many times at different wavelengths and dates. Our tool takes an RA and Dec, finds every SPHEREx image covering it at NASA/IPAC IRSA, cuts out a small field, puts all frames on one pixel grid with one shared brightness scale, and plays them in order. Users can blink two frames, drag a divider between them, subtract one frame from another, or stack frames per detector. Every frame shows its date, detector and wavelength so colour effects are not mistaken for motion.

What it does

  • Query by RA/Dec and field of view (0.02–0.5°), or one click on the five challenge targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis.
  • Time-ordered playback with play/pause, frame stepping and keyboard controls.
  • Viewing modes: sequence, blink A/B, divider, difference (A − B with adjustable gain) and per-detector stack.
  • Filters by detector (1–6) and by wavelength similarity.
  • Metadata on every frame: UTC date, MJD, detector, wavelength and bandwidth, flagged-pixel fraction, source file link.
  • Shareable URLs: the query and view are stored in the address (?ra=&dec=&fov=&detector=).
  • A notes panel that shows pipeline warnings, such as skipped frames or results served from cache.

How it works

  1. The user enters a position or picks a target. The page calls GET /api/frames.
  2. The backend searches IRSA's SIA2 service in the SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 collections for images covering the position.
  3. For each image it downloads only a small cutout through IRSA's cutout service, reads the date, detector and wavelength (from the spectral WCS at the target pixel), and records the flag fraction.
  4. All cutouts are reprojected onto one common TAN grid centred on the target, background-matched by median subtraction, and drawn with one shared asinh stretch, so brightness is comparable between frames.
  5. PNG frames and a JSON manifest are written and cached; the website plays them. Results are cached for 6 hours, and a cached result is served if the archive is down.

Technology

Part

Tools

Frontend

React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS; custom viewer with canvas difference mode

Backend

Python, FastAPI, uvicorn

Astronomy

astropy (FITS, WCS, VOTable, time), reproject, numpy, Pillow

Data access

NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2 search and cutout service

Hosting

One Docker container on Render serving the API, images and built website

Testing

22 offline pytest tests using synthetic FITS files (alignment, shared stretch, moving source, caching, error handling)

Honest science notes

  • We do not claim to have found Planet X or any new object. The tool shows archive images so people can look for motion themselves.
  • Different SPHEREx images are at different wavelengths, so a source can change brightness between frames for spectral reasons alone. The wavelength is shown on every frame.
  • Targets with high proper motion (Barnard's Star, about 10 arcsec per year) are propagated to epoch 2026.0 before querying.
  • Flagged-pixel fraction is a rough indicator, not a quality verdict. We do not mask any flag bits by default because we did not guess which ones are bad.

Current status and limits

  • The website and API are deployed. The offline pipeline is tested. At submission time the live IRSA path was only partly verified: IRSA's search service returned errors (502/503) during our testing, so wavelength extraction on real files and the full five-target run are still to be confirmed. Update this section after the final run.
  • Not built: on-the-fly spectra, a Gaia/WISE overlay (Aladin), and automatic ingestion of new data releases. They are listed as next steps.

Next steps

  • Aperture spectra at the target across all wavelengths (the optional extra challenge item).
  • Gaia and WISE catalogue overlay so users can compare with known sources.
  • Pre-computed frames for all five test targets, so the demo does not depend on archive speed.
  • Automatic pick-up of new SPHEREx releases by adding collection names.

Data, tools and credits

  • SPHEREx images: SPHEREx/JPL-Caltech/NASA, served by NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive.
  • Target positions: SIMBAD, plus the WISE 0855 position given in the challenge brief.
  • Libraries: astropy, reproject, FastAPI, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS.
  • The hero image on the home page is AI-generated for design only and is not telescope data.
